RLxF: Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback

A Few Teacher Steps Go a Long Way: Cost-Efficient On-Policy Data Augmentation for Agent Post-Training

Junze Ye ††thanks: Equal contribution. Contact {junze, miaolu}@stanford.edu, jiayicheng@nyu.edu. Affiliation: Stanford University    Jiayi Cheng Affiliation: New York University    Miao Lu Affiliation: Stanford University    Michal Mankowski Affiliation: New York University    Jose Blanchet Affiliation: Stanford University    Mohsen Bayati Affiliation: Stanford University
Abstract

For LLM agents, supervised fine-tuning is not only about teacher labels’ quality, but also about which interaction contexts those labels condition on. Pure behavioral cloning uses full teacher demonstrations, creating a mismatch between teacher-induced contexts seen in training and student-induced contexts encountered at test time. Recent work addresses this mismatch by querying a teacher at contexts reached by the student, often with increasingly elaborate filtering of the teacher’s continuations. We instead frame on-policy data construction as a budget-allocation problem: under matched supervision resources, should teacher output be spent on more start-to-finish demos, longer continuations, outcome filtering, or broader coverage of learner-induced contexts? We formalize this design space through the rollout policy, switch-time distribution, continuation horizon, filtering rules, and two complementary costs: teacher inference generated before filtering and teacher supervision retained for SFT. Across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench-Dev, bounded unfiltered teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts improve over pure behavioral cloning at matched budgets. On HotpotQA and ALFWorld, where we run the full comparison, few-step continuations match or exceed success-filtered and critical-context-filtered alternatives. Our findings suggest that a few teacher steps, placed at learner-induced contexts, can be a more cost-efficient supervision allocation than longer or more heavily curated teacher completions.

1 Introduction

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains a language-model agent by teacher forcing on labeled assistant turns (Williams and Zipser, 1989). In agent post-training, those labels are often generated by a capable but expensive teacher; the simplest dataset is then a corpus of end-to-end teacher demonstrations. We call this instantiation pure behavioral cloning, or pure BC for short. It is easy to implement, but inherits a familiar weakness from imitation learning: the student is trained on input contexts induced by the teacher, while at test time it acts on contexts induced by its own earlier decisions. For multi-turn agents, an early imperfect action changes the subsequent observation stream, after which the student may see contexts that are poorly represented in the teacher-demonstration corpus. This motivates DAgger-style interactive imitation learning (Ross et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2019), and recent LLM-agent work has adapted the idea by querying a teacher at states reached by the student (Choudhury and Sodhi, 2025; Lyu et al., 2025; Lauffer et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).

Once one collects teacher supervision at learner-induced states, however, the central design question is not simply whether to use “on-policy” data. It is how to allocate a limited supervision budget. Additional teacher output could be spent on more end-to-end teacher demonstrations, longer teacher continuations after a student prefix, outcome-filtered continuations, or bounded corrections spread across more learner-induced states. These choices can all be described as adding supervised data, but their costs are not comparable under a generic unit such as “one training sample.” We therefore propose to track two concrete cost measures: CiC_{\mathrm{i}}, the total teacher inference spent before filtering, and CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}}, the teacher-generated supervision retained and trained on per SFT epoch. This separates protocols that are cheap to generate from those that are cheap to train on after filtering.

A second comparability issue is that even the phrase “randomly sample a learner state” is ambiguous. For episodic LM agents, the relevant state is a learner-induced context generated by a causal hierarchy: first a task prompt is sampled, then a variable-length sequence of interaction turns unfolds, and within each turn the assistant tokens are generated autoregressively with strong serial dependence. Once rollout lengths vary, averaging over this process at the episode level or at the pooled-turn level no longer induces the same context distribution. We make these choices explicit through a unified data-construction framework specifying the rollout policy, switch-time distribution, continuation horizon, filtering rules, and induced context distribution. This framework’s goal is not to introduce a more complex algorithm, but to modularize design choices of on-policy data augmentation protocols.

We then study a stylized one-round augmentation setting. First, train an initial behavioral-cloning checkpoint on a teacher-demonstration corpus 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}. Next, roll out this student on training tasks, sample contexts from the learner-induced trajectories, and ask the teacher to continue from those contexts. Finally, reinitialize from the base student and train on 𝒟BC∪𝒟OP\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OP}}. We call this recipe BC+OP. Our main variant, OP-Short, keeps every sampled teacher continuation but caps it to a small number KK of teacher turns. The continuation length KK controls a breadth-depth tradeoff: a few teacher steps can show local recovery behavior after a student-induced prefix, but longer continuations spend more budget on teacher-descendant contexts rather than on covering additional learner-induced states. We compare OP-Short with Pure-BC, which spends the budget on additional full teacher demonstrations, and with filtered variants OP-Success and OP-Critical, which keep successful teacher continuations and, in the latter case, focus queries on tasks the student fails.

Across HotpotQA (question answering with search tool) (Yang et al., 2018), ALFWorld (text-based embodied planning) (Shridhar et al., 2021), and Terminal-Bench-Dev (command-line coding tasks) (OpenThoughts-Agent Team, 2025), bounded teacher continuations at learner-induced states are a consistently cost-effective form of SFT data augmentation. At matched supervision budgets, OP-Short improves over scaling Pure-BC. On HotpotQA, where we run the full comparison, unfiltered few-step continuations match or exceed the filtered alternatives depending on the cost axis. On ALFWorld and Terminal-Bench-Dev, the best continuation length is larger than in HotpotQA, but additional teacher turns still do not monotonically improve performance. On Terminal-Bench-Dev, OP-Short with a small fraction of the SFT corpus and no reinforcement-learning stage matches the OpenThoughts-Agent baseline that uses the full corpus followed by reinforcement learning.

Our results suggest a practical rule for agent SFT under constrained expert supervision budgets: use pure teacher demonstrations to obtain a reasonable initial student, then allocate additional budget to bounded teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts before investing in full rollouts or heavier filtering. The right continuation length is domain-dependent, but across our experiments a few teacher steps often go a long way. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We formulate SFT data construction for agent post-training as a budget-allocation problem, separating teacher-inference cost CiC_{\mathrm{i}} from retained SFT training cost CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}}.

  2. 2.

    We provide a formal framework for describing on-policy data augmentation that makes explicit the context-generation policy, switch-time distribution, continuation horizon, filtering rules, and how they affect the induced context distribution in variable-length rollouts.

  3. 3.

    We empirically compare bounded unfiltered teacher continuations, filtered continuations, critical-context filtering, and pure behavioral cloning across three agentic benchmarks, finding that a few on-policy teacher steps are often the most cost-effective use of additional teacher supervision.

2 Methods

2.1 Modeling Agentic Interactions as a POMDP

Our experiments involve ReAct-style agents (Yao et al., 2022), each parametrized by an LLM policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. Such an agent interacts with a digital environment by generating assistant turns that optionally contain tool call(s) and receiving environment responses in ChatML format.11 1 Chat Markup Language (ChatML; (OpenAI, 2023)) defines a structured role-annotated LLM context formatting template (e.g. system, user, assistant roles), including serialization protocol. It is widely adopted by open-weight LLMs too. An agent’s goal is to maximize terminally verifiable rewards on a domain-specific collection of tasks 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, split into a training set 𝒬train\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}} and a test set 𝒬test\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{test}} for performance reporting. Specifying the task collection naturally includes a collection of environments and reward functions. We model the aggregate domain-level dynamics as a finite-horizon Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP, (Smallwood and Sondik, 1973; Kaelbling et al., 1998)), denoting it by a tuple ⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒪,Ps,Po,μ,r|Tm​a​x,ℋ⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},\mathrm{P_{s}},\mathrm{P_{o}},\mu,r\,|\,T_{max},\mathcal{H}\rangle. In agentic settings, a task q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} is often identified by its initial state, transition and observation kernels, and reward function; to simplify notation, we mostly suppress this qq-dependence below.

𝒮\mathcal{S} is the latent environment state space. 𝒜\mathcal{A}, or action set, is the text space of producible assistant turns. The observation space 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the text space of one-step environment responses returned by the digital environment and mediated by an agent scaffold.22 2 Also referred to as an “agent harness” in the AI agents literature. See for example (Anthropic, 2026). At turn t>0t>0, a full assistant turn (a token sequence ending at a pre-programmed stop rule) is sampled from the LLM policy,

at∼π(⋅∣ht−1),a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t-1}), (1)

where ht−1∈ℋh_{t-1}\in\mathcal{H} is the LLM-readable context we define later. The environment then evolves according to the transition kernel while the agent scaffold extracts the environment response:

st∼Ps(⋅∣st−1,at),ot∼Po(⋅∣st).s_{t}\sim\mathrm{P_{s}}(\cdot\mid s_{t-1},a_{t}),\qquad o_{t}\sim\mathrm{P_{o}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). (2)

This distributional notation also covers the special case of deterministic digital settings where Ps\mathrm{P_{s}} and/or Po\mathrm{P_{o}} are Dirac delta kernels. A rollout terminates at the stopping time T≤Tm​a​xT\leq T_{max}, either when the assistant turn indicates task completion or when the horizon is reached. We set oT≡∅o_{T}\equiv\varnothing.

Let μ\mu be the empirical distribution over tasks q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}. Drawing q∼μq\sim\mu fixes that task’s initial environment state s0s_{0}, its kernels (Ps,Po)(P_{s},P_{o}), and its reward function rr, so a distribution over tasks and a distribution over s0s_{0} carry the same information in our setting; we write q∼μq\sim\mu throughout. In the basic setting μ\mu is uniform over the task collection under study, and μtrain,μtest\mu_{\mathrm{train}},\mu_{\mathrm{test}} denote its restrictions to 𝒬train,𝒬test\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}},\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{test}}. Reward is terminal: the reward function r:𝒮→[0,1]r:\mathcal{S}\to[0,1] is read only at the terminal environment state, yielding the realized return r:=r⁡(sT)r:=r(s_{T}) with no intermediate reward. This is the RLVR setting, where the environment returns a single verifiable outcome at termination.

A trajectory (τ\tau) is a turn-level, complete-information representation of an agent’s interaction and environment history in a single episode. For a fixed task qq and policy π\pi,

τ0=(q,s0),τt=(q,s0,a1,s1,o1,…,at,st,ot),τ=(q,s0,…,aT,sT,oT,r),\tau_{0}=(q,s_{0}),\;\;\tau_{t}=(q,s_{0},a_{1},s_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t},s_{t},o_{t}),\;\;\tau=(q,s_{0},\ldots,a_{T},s_{T},o_{T},r), (3)

where TT is the terminal turn (i.e. horizon). As an aside, we reserve the word “rollout” for the sampling procedure that runs a policy in the environment and realizes a trajectory. Let ℙqπ\mathbb{P}^{\pi}_{q} denote τ\tau’s probability distribution given a task qq. Given a task distribution μ\mu,

ℙμπ​(τ):=𝔼q∼μ​[ℙqπ​(τ)].\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\pi}(\tau):=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mu}\left[\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\pi}(\tau)\right]. (4)

During the process of rolling out τ\tau, the partial trajectory τt\tau_{t} at each turn t<Tt<T is projected by the agent scaffold to the context state ht∈ℋh_{t}\in\mathcal{H} (“context”). We call such a mapping HH and define:

h0=H⁡(τ0):=(q),ht=H⁡(τt):=ht−1+(at,ot)=(q,a1,o1,…,at,ot).h_{0}=H(\tau_{0}):=(q),\quad h_{t}=H(\tau_{t}):=h_{t-1}+(a_{t},o_{t})=(q,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t},o_{t}). (5)

In addition, given a completed trajectory τ\tau with terminal length TT, we also denote the retrospective construction of hth_{t} by Ht​(τ)H_{t}(\tau), which equals H⁡(τt)H(\tau_{t}) when t≤Tt\leq T, and N/A∉ℋ\mathrm{N/A}\notin\mathcal{H} when t>Tt>T.

Note that a context hth_{t}’s serialized form is the information state the LLM policy π\pi conditions its action on at time tt (Eq. 1), not the latent environment state sts_{t}. Therefore, we use the unmodified “state” to alias context hereafter, referring to “state” and “context” interchangeably. Eq. 5 assumes the agent context extends linearly between turns without truncation or compaction, same in related works like Choudhury and Sodhi (2025) and Lauffer et al. (2025). Appendix G shows a real context in our experiments and its correspondence to this subsection’s notation.

2.2 Context Distribution and the SFT Objective

In the original DAgger paper (Ross et al., 2011), the trajectory stopping time was assumed to be a constant TT, and they instantiated the state distribution (a.k.a. state occupancy measure in the RL theory literature) as a time-uniform distribution dπ​(s)=1T​∑t=1Tdtπ​(s)d^{\pi}(s)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}d^{\pi}_{t}(s), where they hid the μ\mu-dependence and described dtπd^{\pi}_{t} as “the distribution of states at time tt if the learner executed policy π\pi from step 11 to t−1t-1.” We observe that using such a notation to describe episodes with varying lengths, such as in agentic LLM tasks, is under-specified: when TT is random, how could we instantiate the Monte Carlo integration of 𝔼⁡[1T​∑tdtπ]\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}d_{t}^{\pi}]? We try to formalize the inductive biases a practitioner can choose to resolve the “average over what” question.

Recall from (4) and (5) that ℙμπ\mathbb{P}^{\pi}_{\mu} is the trajectory distribution marginalized over μ\mu, and that given a finished trajectory τ\tau, Ht​(τ)∈ℋ∪{N/A}H_{t}(\tau)\in\mathcal{H}\cup\{\mathrm{N/A}\} is the retrospectively constructed context. Define the time-tt marginal context distribution ht∼dμ,tπh_{t}\sim d^{\pi}_{\mu,t}, which implicitly assumes that T⁡(τ)≥tT(\tau)\geq t for the τ\tau that emits hth_{t}, as a trajectory-average counting measure:

dμ,tπ(B):=𝔼τ∼ℙμπ[ 1{Ht−1(τ)∈B}],for any set of contexts B⊆ℋ.d_{\mu,t}^{\pi}(B):=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\pi}}\!\left[\,\mathbf{1}\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\}\,\right],\quad\text{for any set of contexts }B\subseteq\mathcal{H}. (6)

We now introduce a general, any-time context distribution dμπ;wd_{\mu}^{\pi;w}, s.t. h∼dμπ;wh\sim d_{\mu}^{\pi;w} where hh’s turn count t⁡(h)t(h) is jointly sampled. As the POMDP analogue of the state distribution, it is parametrizable by μ\mu, π\pi and a turn-indexed context weighting function wt​(τ)≥0w_{t}(\tau)\geq 0 (ww for short, when unambiguous):

dμπ;w​(B)=𝔼τ∼ℙμπ[∑t=1T⁡(τ)(wt(τ)⋅ 1{Ht−1(τ)∈B})]𝔼τ∼ℙμπ​[∑t=1T⁡(τ)wt​(τ)],for any set of contexts ​B⊆ℋ.d_{\mu}^{\pi;w}(B)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\pi}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\left(w_{t}(\tau)\,\cdot\,\mathbf{1}\left\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\right\}\right)\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\pi}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}w_{t}(\tau)\right]},\quad\text{for any set of contexts }B\subseteq\mathcal{H}. (7)

The choice of wtw_{t} lets Eq. 7 distinguish two state averaging conventions that only coincide when T⁡(τ)T(\tau) is constant with probability 11 for τ∼ℙμπ\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\pi}:

wt​(τ)=1⟶dμπ;𝟏​(B)\displaystyle w_{t}(\tau)=1\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;d_{\mu}^{\pi;\mathbf{1}}(B) :=dμπ;𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥​(B)=𝔼τ[∑t=1T⁡(τ)𝟏{Ht−1(τ)∈B}]𝔼τ​[T​(τ)],\displaystyle:=d_{\mu}^{\pi;\mathbf{pool}}(B)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\mathbf{1}\left\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\right\}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[T(\tau)]}, (8)
wt​(τ)=1T⁡(τ)⟶dμπ;𝟏𝐓​(B)\displaystyle w_{t}(\tau)=\frac{1}{T(\tau)}\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;d_{\mu}^{\pi;\mathbf{\frac{1}{T}}}(B) :=dμπ;𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐣(B)=𝔼τ[1T⁡(τ)∑t=1T⁡(τ)𝟏{Ht−1(τ)∈B}].\displaystyle:=d_{\mu}^{\pi;\mathbf{traj}}(B)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\!\left[\frac{1}{T(\tau)}\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\mathbf{1}\left\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\right\}\right].

The first is pooled-turns randomization: every visited context, regardless of its trajectory, receives equal probability mass after normalization, so longer trajectories contribute more total mass. A fixed-horizon switch sampler with invalid-switch rejection, as in OEC-style random switching, is one implementation that induces this convention; Appendix B.2 gives the derivation. The second is trajectory-uniform randomization: roll out τ\tau until termination, then sample a turn t∼Unif​{1,T⁡(τ)}t\sim\text{Unif}\{1,T(\tau)\}. In this case, every trajectory (episode) receives equal probability mass. The latter is the randomization induced by our uniform-prefix takeover rule used in §3.1 and §3.2.

We now define the SFT objective independently of how the context distribution is induced. Let πe∈Π⋆\pi_{e}\in\Pi^{\star} be a frozen teacher policy and πθ∈ΠΘ\pi_{\theta}\in\Pi^{\mathrm{\Theta}} be the student policy being fine-tuned. For any turn-level context distribution dd over ℋ\mathcal{H}, define the next-turn population SFT objective as the student policy minimizing the forward KL divergence averaged on dd:

ℒSFT(θ;d):=𝔼h∼d[DKL(πe(⋅∣h)∥πθ(⋅∣h))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta;d):=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim d}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{e}(\cdot\mid h)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h)\right)\right]. (9)

Since πe\pi_{e} is fixed, minimizing Eq. 9 is the same as minimizing the dd-averaged cross entropy

ℒ~SFT(θ;d):=𝔼h∼d(𝔼a⋆∼πe(⋅∣h)[−logπθ(a⋆∣h)])\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta;d):=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim d}\left(\mathbb{E}_{a^{\star}\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot\mid h)}\left[-\log\pi_{\theta}(a^{\star}\mid h)\right]\right) (10)

up to an additive constant independent of θ\theta. Here a⋆∈𝒜a^{\star}\in\mathcal{A} is a complete teacher-generated assistant turn, matching our choice of the SFT objective to be next-turn-level: on an interaction context hh, the student is trained to maximize the joint likelihood of teacher’s next assistant turn’s tokens. The single-teacher-turn assumption of Eq. 10 can be easily extended for the case of continuing multiple teacher turns by autoregressive factorization. Appendix B.1 formalizes this multi-turn extension.

dd’s parametrization distinguishes supervision regimes. Standard pure behavioral cloning SFT corresponds to a teacher-induced and pooled-turn context distribution d=dμπe;𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥d=d_{\mu}^{\pi_{e};\mathbf{pool}}, i.e. d=dμπe;wd=d_{\mu}^{\pi_{e};w} with w≡1w\equiv 1. A more “on-policy” supervision scheme, we denote by d=dμρ;wd=d_{\mu}^{\rho;w}, would instead use a context-generating policy ρ≠πe\rho\neq\pi_{e}; ρ\rho can be a student πθ\pi_{\theta}, a teacher-student mixture, or a more complex composition. wt​(τ)w_{t}(\tau) offers another flexible knob to configure dd: besides the two tt-agnostic instances in Eq. 8, it may be beneficial for future work to explore wt​(τ)w_{t}(\tau) as a per-context-turn value function. Lastly, μ\mu may be instantiated as the empirical distribution over a finite task collection.

2.3 The Budget Allocation Problem in Fine-Tuning Dataset Construction

Separate from the sequential decision process of an LLM’s rollout, researchers face a different decision problem when post-training it for downstream applications: how to allocate a given fine-tuning resource budget to maximize final performance on the test set. In this paper, the teacher is an advanced LLM whose model size and inference cost are much larger than the student’s, but it can be instantiated as a human expert too. We quantify the budget constraint in two separate axes:

  1. 1.

    CiC_{\mathrm{i}}: Total teacher inference cost, before custom data filtering

  2. 2.

    CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}}: Per-epoch training cost, i.e. GPU hours needed on the (filtered) SFT traces

Both CiC_{\mathrm{i}} and CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} are measurable either in tokens or the number assistant turns generated by the teacher. For CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}}, the GPU hours needed by an SFT training run is roughly proportional to the number of accepted teacher tokens on an epoch-normalized basis. Whether the spending on CiC_{\mathrm{i}} or CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} dominates a research team’s fine-tuning budget concern, we suppose, is often idiosyncratic. For example, a research group with a dedicated allocation on a large GPU cluster faces near-zero marginal training cost, so they would be far more cost-sensitive to external API inference calls (CiC_{\mathrm{i}}) needed to generate teacher completions than to the size of the resulting training corpus (CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}}). So rather than assigning an ad-hoc weight, our experiments visualize budget scaling under each extreme point respectively.

Beyond inference and training compute, task diversity in 𝒬train\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}, which we proxy by |𝒬train||\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|, also shapes a student’s learning efficiency; recall from §2.1 that (μ,Ps,Po,r)(\mu,\mathrm{P_{s}},\mathrm{P_{o}},r) is often implemented as an empirical distribution over 𝒬train\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}. To avoid confounding effect from this factor, we generally control |𝒬train||\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}| when comparing among OP and pure BC variants, so differences along the cost axes isolate the effect of the data-construction recipe alone. Any variation in |𝒬train||\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}| is explicitly indicated in a plot. We treat |𝒬train||\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}| as a hyperparameter rather than a third budget axis since it is often much more expensive and inelastic than CiC_{\mathrm{i}} and CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}}: the pool of domain-specific training tasks with verifiable answers is typically determined by whatever open-source or proprietary datasets are available at the fine-tuning phase’s onset, and meaningfully expanding its coverage requires highly costly human annotation effort that is qualitatively different from scaling teacher inference or GPU compute.

2.4 Design Space of Fine-Tuning Dataset Construction

We present a common recipe to connect implementation-level data curation knobs to the population SFT objective in Eq. 10. In code, these knobs are easily mutable objects compatible with LLM post-training libraries like verl or LlamaFactory: the policy checkpoint generating prefix contexts, the switch-time sampler, the prefix-context and continuation filters, the teacher-continuation horizon, etc. Connecting the formalism in §2.1-§2.3, choosing these objects instantiates the empirical context distribution corresponding to a population distribution dd and to deciding how much teacher inference CiC_{\mathrm{i}} and accepted training signal CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} are spent to approximate it.

Let ρ\rho be the prefix-context policy and πe\pi_{e} the teacher labeler. A general implementation recipe is

𝒢:=(ρ,πe,n,Ψ,𝒯switch,K,Φ),\mathcal{G}:=(\rho,\pi_{e},n,\Psi,\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}},K,\Phi), (11)

where nn is the number of SFT context-continuation traces proposed per task, Ψ\Psi is a prefix-context filter applied before teacher continuation, 𝒯switch\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}} is a protocol to sample a candidate switch time t′t^{\prime}, KK caps the number of teacher assistant turns in the continuation, and Φ\Phi is a post-continuation filter. The realized count of accepted traces NN is therefore random and can be smaller than n⋅|𝒬train|n\cdot|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|. For each trace proposal on task qq, first the context-generating policy is rolled out to produce a trajectory τ∼ℙqρ\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\rho} and either t′∼𝒯switch​(τ)t^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}}(\tau) or t′∼𝒯switcht^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}} independently of τ\tau.

If t′≤T⁡(τ)t^{\prime}\leq T(\tau) and Ψ⁡(τ,t′)=1\Psi(\tau,t^{\prime})=1, the proposal is explored further: the (partial) trajectory up to the t′t^{\prime}-th turn induces the prefix context ht′−1=H⁡(τt′−1)h_{t^{\prime}-1}=H(\tau_{t^{\prime}-1}). The teacher continues the interaction from H⁡(τt′−1)H(\tau_{t^{\prime}-1}) and its associated state st′−1s_{t^{\prime}-1} for k′≤Kk^{\prime}\leq K assistant turns before finish. We denote the aggregate trajectory including the continuation, which may be rejected by the filter Φ\Phi, by

τ~=(q,s0,a1,s1,o1,…,at′−1,st′−1,ot′−1,at′⋆,st′,ot′,…,at′+k′−1⋆),\widetilde{\tau}=(q,s_{0},a_{1},s_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t^{\prime}-1},s_{t^{\prime}-1},o_{t^{\prime}-1},a^{\star}_{t^{\prime}},s_{t^{\prime}},o_{t^{\prime}},\ldots,a^{\star}_{t^{\prime}+k^{\prime}-1}), (12)

where starred actions are teacher-generated. Note that under the linear-context, no-format-change convention of Eq. 5, H⁡(τt′−1)=H⁡(τ~t′−1)H(\tau_{t^{\prime}-1})=H(\widetilde{\tau}_{t^{\prime}-1}). If the teacher and student scaffolds use different chat templates and tokenizers, the teacher will see H⁡(τt′−1)H(\tau_{t^{\prime}-1}) serialized in its own format, though the accepted continuation would be rendered in the student’s format before SFT. Altogether, the post-filter SFT dataset is the collection of context-continuation traces with superscript ii as index:

𝒟𝒢:={(Hti′−1(τi),H(τ~i)[ti′:]):i=1,…,N},\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{G}}:=\{(H_{t^{\prime}_{i}-1}(\tau^{i}),\,H(\widetilde{\tau}^{i})[t^{\prime}_{i}:]):i=1,\ldots,N\}, (13)

where [ti′:][t^{\prime}_{i}:] is an array slicing notation for the teacher-generated continuation segment. The SFT loss is computed only on teacher-generated assistant turns (a⋅⋆a^{\star}_{\cdot}) in the continuation, excluding environment observations. Eq. 13 cleanly expresses the intended separation: ρ\rho supplies the prefix context and πe\pi_{e} supplies the continuation. Algorithm 1 summarizes the overall procedure of constructing 𝒟𝒢\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{G}}.

The way 𝒯switch\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}} samples t′t^{\prime} implicitly defines the context weighting function ww in Eq. 7 and 8. If τ\tau is first completed and then t′∼Unif⁡{1,…,T⁡(τ)}t^{\prime}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T(\tau)\}, the induced context distribution is trajectory-uniform, dμρ;trajd^{\rho;\mathrm{traj}}_{\mu} and w≡1/T⁡(τ)w\equiv 1/T(\tau). If instead t′∼Unif⁡{1,…,Tm​a​x}t^{\prime}\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T_{max}\}, i.e. a fixed support, and the pair (τ,t′)(\tau,t^{\prime}) is rejected when t′>T⁡(τ)t^{\prime}>T(\tau), then the accepted contexts follow the pooled-turn distribution dμρ;poold^{\rho;\mathrm{pool}}_{\mu} with w≡1w\equiv 1; in other words, tasks and rollouts with shorter horizons naturally are less represented in accepted examples. Lauffer et al. (2025)’s implementation resembles dμρ;poold^{\rho;\mathrm{pool}}_{\mu}: it samples a switch index before the rollout, lets the student act until either the switch is reached or the student terminates, and discards trajectories that terminate before the teacher takes over (§B.2).

When 𝒯switch≡1\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}}\equiv 1, (ρ,K,n)=(πe,Tm​a​x,1)(\rho,K,n)=(\pi_{e},T_{max},1), and no filters, we call 𝒟𝒢\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{G}} “pure BC” and alias by 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}. We define the policy initialized from a base student checkpoint π0\pi_{0} then fine-tuned on 𝒟𝒢\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{G}} as

π1:=SFT⁡(π0,𝒟BC).\pi_{1}:=\mathrm{SFT}(\pi_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}). (14)

We call 𝒟𝒢\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{G}} “on-policy” and write it as 𝒟OP\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OP}} when ρ∈ΠΘ\rho\in\Pi_{\Theta} and ρ≠πe\rho\neq\pi_{e}, for example with ρ=π1\rho=\pi_{1}. In the BC+OP recipes, the final supervised run is reinitialized from π0\pi_{0} and trained on 𝒟BC∪𝒟OP\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OP}}; the context-generating policy that generated 𝒟OP\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OP}} is fixed during this data-generation round.

Table 1 shows four types of 𝒢=(ρ,πe,n,Ψ,𝒯switch,K,Φ)\mathcal{G}=(\rho,\pi_{e},n,\Psi,\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}},K,\Phi) our experiments study. Pure-BC uses nn as a data scaling lever; intuitively, more teacher traces per task offer a lower variance estimation of the KL term in Eq. 9. OP-Short accepts every sampled prefix context and continuation, but uses a small KK. OP-Success sets K=Tm​a​xK=T_{max} and accepts only teacher continuations with verifiably correct answers; it is similar to OEC’s rejection sampling setup, and the success-only filter makes CiC_{\mathrm{i}} larger per accepted trace as a teacher may not always be accepted. OP-Critical adds the prefix-context filter Ψ(τ,t′)=𝟙{r(τ)=0}\Psi(\tau,t^{\prime})=\mathds{1}\{r(\tau)=0\} in our experiments, so teacher budget is spent only on tasks the rollout policy ρ\rho fails to solve on its own.

3 Experiments

We test the cost-and-performance framing of §2 on three distinct agentic environments. On HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) (search-based question answering) we compare all four recipe types in Table 1, including varying KK for OP-Short and nn for Pure-BC. On ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) (embodied household planning in text environments) we compare OP-Short at K=3K=3 to pure BC at four training-instance budgets, with in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation, an ablation on the ratio of on-policy to expert-prefix data. On Terminal-Bench-Dev (OpenThoughts-Agent Team, 2025) (solving code problems in an interactive shell) we sweep pure BC across five fractions of the BC corpus and run OP-Short at two continuation budgets across three prefix policies, and compare with the OpenThoughts-Agent baseline. For the three OP types in all our experiments, ρ\rho is π1\pi_{1} from Eq. 14, and the final augmented SFT set is 𝒟BC∪𝒟OP\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OP}} (the same 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}} used to obtain π1\pi_{1}).

3.1 Search Agent: HotpotQA

HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) was originally designed to test a model’s ability to answer a question by synthesizing evidence from preset Wikipedia snippets. We use the Search-R1 + VeRL adaptation (Jin et al., 2025; Sheng et al., 2025), which removes the preset snippets and turns each question (i.e. task) into a sequential interaction with a searchable database: the agent interleaves thinking with search queries to a 2018 snapshot of the English Wikipedia, receives retrieved passages as observations, and terminates by submitting an answer in no more than Tmax=5T_{\mathrm{max}}=5 turns. Since this database is static, the environment state sts_{t} is time-invariant; the rollout’s meaningful evolution is the LLM-readable context hth_{t} as tool calls and observations accumulate. The student is initialized from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (π0\pi_{0}), the teacher is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (πe\pi_{e}). pass@1 is normalized exact match against the official references, following Search-R1’s GitHub implementation.

Figure 2 fixes |𝒬train|=1000|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|=1000 medium-level HotpotQA questions and varies only the SFT trace construction recipe. Pure-BC scales by increasing nn, while OP-Short scales by increasing the teacher turns limit KK. For all OP variants, ρ=π1\rho=\pi_{1}, corresponding to Figure 2’s leftmost purple Pure-BC point. We roll out ρ\rho for n=3n=3 times per question, sample 𝒯switch\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{switch}} uniformly over each completed trajectory, and train on πe\pi_{e}’s continuation from the resulting student-induced context. This directly instantiates the trajectory-uniform distribution dμπ1;𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐣d_{\mu}^{\pi_{1};\mathbf{traj}} from Eq. 8. All variants use the same retriever, system prompt, and a temperature of 11 for data generation and evaluation.

To avoid selecting noisy test-set wins, the learning rate and final SFT checkpoint are chosen using held-out HotpotQA dev runs before final test evaluation; Figure 6 reports the training hyperparameters and checkpoint selection process.

On-policy supervisions improve SFT sample efficiency. On both cost axes in Figure 2, teacher completions from π1\pi_{1}-induced prefixes make better use of the fixed question set than additional Pure-BC demonstrations. Pure-BC improves as more complete teacher traces are added but enters a region of diminishing returns, whereas the OP recipes achieve higher pass@1 at comparable supervision budgets, suggesting that once naive scaling of expert demonstrations saturates, redirecting teacher supervision toward student-induced contexts offers a higher marginal return per token spent.

Scaling teacher continuation length has non-monotone returns. The OP-Short KK-sweep shows that longer teacher continuations are not automatically better, even before cost normalization. Increasing KK helps up to K=3K=3, but K=5K=5 is worse despite spending more teacher tokens. This non-monotonicity likely reflects two factors: the main learning is the bounded repair at the student-induced state, beyond which extra turns produce completions unlikely for a student; and in HotpotQA, trajectories that exhaust all TmaxT_{\mathrm{max}} might correlate with more ill-posed questions, biasing long continuations to be less instructional.

Filtering trades teacher inference for fewer training tokens. The filtered recipes, OP-Success and OP-Critical, can look attractive on retained training cost CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} because rejected continuations are not trained on. They are less favorable on teacher-inference cost CiC_{\mathrm{i}}, where rejected teacher tokens are still charged. The gap between the two panels therefore clarifies the tradeoff: filtering is most useful when the SFT training compute is scarce, not when teacher inference is the binding resource.

3.2 Embodied Agent: ALFWorld

We use Qwen3-0.6B as the student and Qwen3-8B (after RL) as the teacher. Following the official splits, we train on train (∼\sim3500 tasks) and evaluate on valid_seen. We compare the pure BC against OP-Short with K∈{1,5,∞}K\in\{1,5,\infty\}, OP-Success, and OP-Critical, while sweeping the unique training tasks count |𝒬train|∈{64,128,256}|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|\in\{64,128,256\}. We also fine-tune the student using a subsequent RL stage, initialized from the |𝒬train|=128|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|{=}128 pure BC and OP-Short checkpoints and uses the remaining train task. SFT uses learning rate 5×10−55{\times}10^{-5}, batch size 1616, and 88 epochs; GRPO uses learning rate 1×10−61{\times}10^{-6}, batch size 1616, group size 88, and 44 epochs. The SFT stage result is shown in Figure 3. OP-Short is consistently above the Pure BC curve at similar teacher-supervision budgets, showing that on-policy data augmentation enjoys better sample efficiency.

Fewer teacher steps could be more cost-effective and sample-efficient than full teacher completions. We conduct ablation experiments on the number of teacher continuation steps. Figure 3 shows that longer teacher continuations do not monotonically improve ALFWorld performance. For all of task budgets |𝒬train|∈{64,128,256}|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|\in\{64,128,256\}, the best short-continuation runs occur at K=5K=5 and outperform the corresponding K=∞K=\infty runs despite spending fewer teacher tokens. Filtering shows the same cost tradeoff: once the discarded teacher continuations are counted as labeling cost (See Figure 3 left), the filtered variants do not necessarily deliver a consistent pass@1 gain matching their extra teacher inference tokens spend. Therefore, after a few corrective teacher actions, additional budget is often better spent on covering more student states than on extending more continuation.

Ablation on optimal mixing ratio. Given a fixed teacher supervision budget, we also study the optimal mixture of the BC data (induce the on-policy student state distribution as well as part of the final training data) and on-policy data. Figure 4 sweeps the ratio between expert-prefix data and on-policy-prefix data under three total teacher-supervision budgets. Across three fully swept budgets 147K, 296K, and 562K, allocating a nonzero fraction to on-policy prefixes (i.e., OP-Short) is better than pure expert-prefix supervision (Pure BC), but using only on-policy data is also suboptimal. The intuition is that it is better for the student to start approaching the desired state distribution before collecting on-policy data. The best observed on-policy ratios are about 90%90\%, 50%50\%, and 90%90\% for the three token budgets, respectively, indicating that the optimal mixture can depend on the total supervision budget. This pattern suggests that on-policy data should be treated as targeted augmentation rather than a replacement for expert demonstrations: expert-prefix data provides stable coverage of canonical traces, while on-policy-prefix data corrects the student on states induced by its own errors.

3.3 Coding Agent: Terminal-Bench-Dev

We use Qwen3-8B as the student and GLM-4.6 as the teacher, following the OpenThoughts-Agent project (OpenThoughts-Agent Team, 2025). The BC corpus 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}} is OpenThoughts-Agent-v1-SFT (OpenThoughts-Agent Team, 2025), which contains 15,209 teacher traces on nl2bash (Lin et al., 2018) and inferredbugs (Jin et al., 2023). We evaluate our SFT data curation strategies on Terminal-Bench-Dev (70 questions total) for direct comparability to the OT-Agent baselines.

We shuffle the trajectories in 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}, and then our pure BC baselines are trained on the first {10%,25%,50%,75%,100%}\{10\%,25\%,50\%,75\%,100\%\} portion of the shuffled 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}} (1,520 to 15,209 traces) such that each larger SFT train set fully contains the preceding ones. OP-Short is run at two continuation budgets, K=3K=3 and K=∞K=\infty with no outcome filter. The mean score we report in Figure 5 is the average of the official OT-Agent codebase’s verifier scores over 70×3=21070\times 3=210 trials, i.e. the 70-question TB-dev set was attempted three times independently to capture response variance.

OP-Short matches the post-RL OpenThoughts-Agent baseline at one-tenth the BC budget. At a matched fraction of the corpus size, OP-Short improves substantially over pure BC: finetuning with 10%10\% of 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}, pure BC reaches 11.4%11.4\% TB-dev, while OP-Short at K=3K=3 reaches 16.0%16.0\% and 19.0%19.0\%, surpassing the OpenThoughts-Agent post-RL baseline of 17.3%17.3\% that uses the full 15,20915{,}209 BC traces followed by 720720 GRPO tasks. On this benchmark on-policy data construction, applied at the SFT stage and without any RL, recovers the gain that the OpenThoughts-Agent recipe extracts from a combination of full-corpus SFT and subsequent RL.

Hyperparameters and more ablation experiments, including pure On-Policy cases and the scenario where tasks in BC and On-Policy data are different, are shown in Table 4 and 5 in Appendix F. For OP-Short we additionally vary the prefix policy across three checkpoints, the untrained student π0\pi_{0} and the BC checkpoints trained on 10%10\% and 100%100\% of 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{BC}}, holding questions and number of traces in 𝒟OP\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{OP}} identical across prefix choices. Our observations still hold under different circumstances.

4 Discussion

The main practical lesson is not that “on-policy” data should replace pure behavioral cloning. Rather, it is useful as targeted augmentation once BC has produced a student whose mistakes define informative contexts. In this view, the key knob is how much teacher-descendant trajectory to buy at each learner-induced context state. Our results suggest that bounded continuations often provide enough local recovery signal, while spending the same budget on longer completions, additional full demonstrations, or success filtering can reduce coverage of distinct student states. The continuation budget KK should therefore be treated as a domain-dependent breadth–depth parameter, not a universal constant. Filtering should likewise be chosen according to the binding cost axis: it can reduce retained SFT tokens, but rejected continuations still consume teacher inference.

Limitations.

We study one-round augmentation on three verifiable agentic benchmarks, with the most complete variant comparison on HotpotQA and ALFWorld. The conclusions may change for long-horizon tasks where recovery requires extended planning, for settings without automatic reward verification, or under iterative data collection. We also do not provide a theory predicting the optimal KK or the observed non-monotone returns to continuation length.

Appendix A Related Work

DAgger and on-policy SFT.

Our work builds on interactive imitation learning, especially DAgger [Ross and Bagnell, 2010, Ross et al., 2011, Ross and Bagnell, 2014, Kelly et al., 2019], which reduces compounding error by collecting expert labels at learner-induced states. Caccia et al. [2024] show that, for LLM agents, better prediction on expert trajectories need not translate to better downstream performance once the student acts on its own induced contexts, and mention DAgger as a potential remedy. Lauffer et al. [2025] are the closest prior work to our intervention-style setup: they roll in with the student to a random switch step, let the expert continue to termination, mask the student prefix during training, and filter by verifiable success and student repetition. This motivates our filtered baselines, whereas our main OP-SHORT method keeps every sampled continuation but bounds it to a few teacher turns. Other variants use privileged train-time teacher state [Choudhury and Sodhi, 2025], teacher-identified first-error corrections [Lyu et al., 2025], self-reflected teacher-guided corrections [Chen et al., 2025a], or turn-level teacher-student mixing for long-horizon software agents [Li et al., 2026]. Related methods also address trajectory-level error accumulation through step-level comparison [Wang et al., 2025], teacher-free first-error revision [Yuan et al., 2025], or off-policy selection of critical trajectory segments [Chen et al., 2025b, Lan et al., 2025].

On-policy distillation.

A related line studies on-policy distillation (OPD) for autoregressive language models, training on student-sampled sequences while matching teacher behavior via generalized knowledge distillation [Agarwal et al., 2024], reverse-KL objectives [Gu et al., 2024], context internalization [Ye et al., 2026], privileged self-distillation [Zhao et al., 2026b], verbal-score supervision [Xiong et al., 2026], or black-box discriminator-based distillation [Ye et al., 2025]. Concurrently, Zhao et al. [2026a] decouple prefix source from KL direction, identifying student-prefix forward-KL as DAgger-style on-policy SFT and student-prefix reverse-KL as OPD. Our setting focuses on explicit teacher completions at executable, learner-visited agent states; this is natural for multi-turn tool-use, supports black-box teachers, and lets us measure the budget in generated and retained teacher tokens rather than in token-level distribution queries.

Rejection-sampling SFT and the SFT-as-RL connection.

A complementary line analyzes outcome-filtered SFT in its own right. Qin and Springenberg [2025] show that SFT on success-filtered trajectories optimizes a lower bound on the sparse-reward RL objective and propose an importance-weighted variant that tightens this bound. This perspective varies which generated trajectories are retained; we additionally vary the state distribution by querying the teacher at learner-induced prefix states. Accordingly, we treat filtered SFT as one data-construction choice within a broader budget-allocation problem, rather than only as a stand-alone alternative to RL.

Positioning relative to prior work.

Recent agent post-training recipes often bundle several choices: prefix policy, switch-time sampling, continuation length, masking, filtering, and sometimes a subsequent RL stage. We instead make these choices explicit and compare them under matched supervision resources, separating teacher-inference cost from retained SFT training cost. This isolates the question central to our experiments: once a reasonable behavioral-cloning student is available, whether additional teacher budget is better spent on more start-to-end expert demonstrations, longer or filtered teacher continuations, or short unfiltered corrections spread over more learner-induced contexts.

Appendix B Mathematical Details

B.1 Multi-turn teacher continuations and the SFT objective

§2.2 defines the population SFT objective at the single-next-turn level. We now spell out how the same objective can be revised to model SFT on multi-turn continuations for §2.4 recipes with K>1K>1.

One notational distinction is useful before defining the multi-turn objective. In the single-next-turn objective of Eq. 10, a sample from dd only needs to specify an LLM-readable context hh, since the teacher action is used as a supervised label and need not be executed. For a multi-turn teacher continuation, however, the teacher’s first action must be executed to produce the next observation, so the sampled object must also contain a replayable environment state. We therefore let d¯\bar{d} denote a distribution over executable partial trajectories, which include replicable environment snapshots, whose context pushforward recovers the main-text context distribution dd:

H#​d¯=d,τt−1∼d¯,ht−1=H⁡(τt−1).H_{\#}\bar{d}=d,\qquad\tau_{t-1}\sim\bar{d},\qquad h_{t-1}=H(\tau_{t-1}). (15)

In our digital agent environments, such as HotpotQA, ALFWorld, Terminal-Bench, and SWE-Bench-style settings, this replayable prefix is typically stored or reconstructed losslessly from the task seed, scaffold state, and action history; this is much easier to re-simulate than in physical environments, where replaying a trajectory may introduce non-trivial sensor and environment variation.

Consider a partial trajectory τt−1\tau_{t-1} with LLM-readable context ht−1=H⁡(τt−1)h_{t-1}=H(\tau_{t-1}). A teacher continuation from this context consists of at most KK subsequent teacher turns and environment observations,

y≥t=(at⋆,ot,…,at+L−1⋆,ot+L−1),L≤K,y_{\geq t}=(a_{t}^{\star},o_{t},\ldots,a_{t+L-1}^{\star},o_{t+L-1}),\qquad L\leq K, (16)

where LL is a random variable that is completely determined by y≥ty_{\geq t}’s realization and may be much smaller than KK if the episode terminates early. We write

y≥t∼CeK(⋅∣τt−1)y_{\geq t}\sim C_{e}^{K}(\cdot\mid\tau_{t-1}) (17)

for the distribution over such continuations obtained by repeatedly sampling teacher actions and stepping the environment:

at+j⋆∼πe(⋅∣ht+j−1),st+j∼Ps(⋅∣st+j−1,at+j⋆),ot+j∼Po(⋅∣st+j),a_{t+j}^{\star}\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot\mid h_{t+j-1}),\qquad s_{t+j}\sim\mathrm{P}_{s}(\cdot\mid s_{t+j-1},a_{t+j}^{\star}),\qquad o_{t+j}\sim\mathrm{P}_{o}(\cdot\mid s_{t+j}), (18)

for j=0,…,L−1j=0,\ldots,L-1, and the context extended as

ht+j=H⁡(τt+j)=ht+j−1+(at+j⋆,ot+j).h_{t+j}=H(\tau_{t+j})=h_{t+j-1}+(a_{t+j}^{\star},o_{t+j}). (19)

Thus CeKC_{e}^{K} is the closed-loop continuation operator induced by the teacher policy, the environment dynamics, the observation kernel, and the stopping rule. A completion filter Φ\Phi re-weights this continuation law by rejecting some continuations. We denote the accepted traces’ law by CeK,ΦC_{e}^{K,\Phi}.

From the student policy’s perspective, the likelihood of a continuation y≥ty_{\geq t} factors sequentially as

pθ​(y≥t∣τt−1)=∏j=0L−1πθ​(at+j⋆∣ht+j−1)⋅Ps​(st+j∣st+j−1,at+j⋆)⋅Po​(ot+j∣st+j).p_{\theta}(y_{\geq t}\mid\tau_{t-1})=\prod_{j=0}^{L-1}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t+j}^{\star}\mid h_{t+j-1})\cdot\mathrm{P}_{s}(s_{t+j}\mid s_{t+j-1},a_{t+j}^{\star})\cdot\mathrm{P}_{o}(o_{t+j}\mid s_{t+j}). (20)

The environment transition and observation terms do not depend on θ\theta. Therefore, up to an additive constant independent of θ\theta, the negative log-likelihood of an accepted continuation is

ℓsft(θ;τt−1,y≥t)=∑j=0L−1−logπθ(at+j⋆∣ht+j−1).\ell_{\mathrm{sft}}(\theta;\tau_{t-1},y_{\geq t})=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t+j}^{\star}\mid h_{t+j-1}). (21)

Equivalently, the multi-turn population SFT objective induced by a replayable prefix distribution d¯\bar{d} and an accepted teacher-continuation law is

ℒ~sftK,Φ(θ;d¯)=𝔼τt−1∼d¯[𝔼y≥t∼CeK,Φ(⋅∣τt−1)[∑j=0L⁡(y≥t)−1−logπθ(at+j⋆∣ht+j−1)]].\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{sft}}^{K,\Phi}(\theta;\bar{d})=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{t-1}\sim\bar{d}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{y_{\geq t}\sim C_{e}^{K,\Phi}(\cdot\mid\tau_{t-1})}\left[\sum_{j=0}^{L(y_{\geq t})-1}-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t+j}^{\star}\mid h_{t+j-1})\right]\right]. (22)

This expression should be read at the turn level: each at+j⋆a_{t+j}^{\star} is a complete assistant turn, whose cross entropy is implemented as a sum over its per-token log probabilities. The summation over jj does not assume that the teacher turns within y≥ty_{\geq t} are independent. Rather, it is the sequential factorization of the likelihood under teacher forcing, where each later context is obtained by appending the earlier teacher action and environment observation.

For K=1K=1, only the pushforward context distribution d=H#​d¯d=H_{\#}\bar{d} matters and this reduces to the next-turn objective in Eq. 10. For K>1K>1, the first loss term supervises the student at the sampled context ht−1h_{t-1}, while later terms supervise the student at teacher-descendant contexts induced by the same continuation. Thus increasing KK trades broader coverage of sampled contexts for deeper teacher recovery from each sampled context.

B.2 Unif​{1,…,Tm​a​x}\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T_{max}\} switching with invalid-switch rejection induces pooled-turn sampling

This appendix justifies the pooled-turn statement for the proposal-budget convention used in Algorithm 1. Consider one switch proposal. Sample a task q∼μq\sim\mu, roll out the context-generating policy to obtain τ∼ℙqρ\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\rho} with stopping time T⁡(τ)≤TmaxT(\tau)\leq T_{\mathrm{max}}, and independently sample U∼Unif⁡{1,…,Tmax}U\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T_{\mathrm{max}}\}. Accept the proposal iff U≤T⁡(τ)U\leq T(\tau); otherwise no prefix context exists at that turn and the proposal is discarded. For any measurable set of contexts B⊆ℋB\subseteq\mathcal{H},

ℙ⁡{HU−1​(τ)∈B∣U≤T⁡(τ)}\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\{H_{U-1}(\tau)\in B\mid U\leq T(\tau)\} =𝔼q∼μ,τ∼ℙqρ[∑t=1T⁡(τ)1Tmax𝟏{Ht−1(τ)∈B}]𝔼q∼μ,τ∼ℙqρ​[∑t=1T⁡(τ)1Tmax]\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mu,\,\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\rho}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{max}}}\mathbf{1}\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mu,\,\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\rho}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{max}}}\right]} (23)
=𝔼τ∼ℙμρ[∑t=1T⁡(τ)𝟏{Ht−1(τ)∈B}]𝔼τ∼ℙμρ​[T​(τ)]=dμρ;pool​(B).\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\rho}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\mathbf{1}\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\rho}}[T(\tau)]}=d^{\rho;\mathrm{pool}}_{\mu}(B). (24)

Thus sampling a global-horizon switch and rejecting switches that occur after the realized trajectory terminates induces the same accepted prefix-context distribution as the pooled-turn convention of Eq. 8. With an empirical task set and nn proposal attempts per task, the same calculation applies with μ\mu equal to the uniform empirical distribution over 𝒬train\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}. Tasks whose realized rollouts are shorter simply produce fewer accepted proposals in expectation, since ℙ⁡(U≤T⁡(τ)∣τ)=T⁡(τ)/Tmax\mathbb{P}(U\leq T(\tau)\mid\tau)=T(\tau)/T_{\mathrm{max}}.

This equivalence isolates invalid-switch rejection. The prefix-context filter Ψ\Psi and post-continuation filter Φ\Phi in the recipe intentionally reweight the accepted distribution. For example, let pΦ​(τ,t)p_{\Phi}(\tau,t) be the probability that a teacher continuation from prefix context Ht−1​(τ)H_{t-1}(\tau) passes the post-continuation filter. After applying Ψ\Psi and Φ\Phi, the accepted prefix-context distribution becomes

𝔼τ∼ℙμρ[∑t=1T⁡(τ)Ψ(τ,t)pΦ(τ,t) 1{Ht−1(τ)∈B}]𝔼τ∼ℙμρ​[∑t=1T⁡(τ)Ψ⁡(τ,t)​pΦ​(τ,t)].\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\rho}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\Psi(\tau,t)\,p_{\Phi}(\tau,t)\,\mathbf{1}\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}^{\rho}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\Psi(\tau,t)\,p_{\Phi}(\tau,t)\right]}. (25)

Invalid-switch rejection alone gives dμρ;poold^{\rho;\mathrm{pool}}_{\mu}; additional filters produce the corresponding filtered pooled-turn distribution.

As an aside, the above proposal-budget convention is different from topping up every task to the same number of accepted switches. If one resamples until each task has nn accepted prefix contexts, invalid-switch rejection instead induces the equal-task average of per-task pooled distributions,

1|𝒬train|​∑q∈𝒬train𝔼τ∼ℙqρ[∑t=1T⁡(τ)𝟏{Ht−1(τ)∈B}]𝔼τ∼ℙqρ​[T​(τ)],\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{train}}}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\rho}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T(\tau)}\mathbf{1}\{H_{t-1}(\tau)\in B\}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbb{P}_{q}^{\rho}}[T(\tau)]}, (26)

which coincides with the global pooled-turn law only when expected horizons are constant across tasks or when the task distribution is reweighted accordingly. More generally, if U∼νU\sim\nu for a fixed distribution on {1,…,Tmax}\{1,\ldots,T_{\mathrm{max}}\}, the accepted prefix-context distribution is the corresponding ν\nu-weighted turn distribution; the uniform case above is exactly pooled-turn sampling.

Appendix C Compute Resources

All HotpotQA SFT and GRPO experiments were run on a single H100 node with 8 GPU cards and 64 CPUs; the Wikipedia document retriever tool was co-located with the verl trainer setup. The Qwen3-235B teacher model was queried via API calls through OpenRouter. All ALFWorld SFT and GRPO experiments were run on a two H100 GPU cards and 64 CPUs. Most of Terminal-Bench-Dev SFT tasks were run on a single A100 node with 4 GPUs and 64 CPUs. Some tasks were run on a single H100 node with 4 GPUs and 64 CPUs. The GLM 4.6 teacher model was queried via API calls through OpenRouter. Virtual sandboxes were accessed through Daytona.

Appendix D HotpotQA

D.1 Training Setup

All HotpotQA experiments use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the student model, trained on a single node with 8×\times H100 GPUs via the verl framework [Sheng et al., 2025] with FSDP2 sharding in BF16 mixed precision. Gradient checkpointing is enabled throughout. Full-parameter finetuning is used. Table 2 lists the SFT hyperparameters. Each iteration fine-tunes the latest checkpoint for 3 epochs over the accumulated correction dataset, and an author manually reviews the validation loss to select the checkpoint with the lowest loss.

D.2 HotpotQA Model Checkpoint Selection

In this section, we show how we selection SFT model checkpoints from the results in Figure 6. We compare pass@@1 performance on 3k medium problems in many different cases to get the model checkpoint to use for later experiments.

Appendix E ALFWorld

E.1 Training Setup

ALFWorld experiments are also built upon VeRL repo. We detail the experiment configs for SFT in Table 3.

Appendix F Terminal-Bench-Dev

This section describes the SFT training details in Section 3.3, see Table 4. The hyperparameters work for all the SFT training process we mentioned, including the pure BC SFT process, as well as OP and BC+OP experiments. This training pipeline is inherited from OpenThoughts-Agent Team [OpenThoughts-Agent Team, 2025] with light modifications to make fair comparison.

F.1 Terminal-Bench-Dev extra experiments

Table 5 shows all TB-dev experiment results in different settings. First two pure OP results validates our conclusion that the optimal continuation length should be set with the task horizon and is not a fixed number. The BC+OP with different tasks experiment is more alike to OEC [Lauffer et al., 2025]. The result show that this data mixture also works on Qwen3-8B, different from OEC which SFT on the prefix model directly. And our RL result shows training and do RL directly on student model can outperform reported RL result from OpenThoughts-Agent team. We would like to mention that our method is not exclusive to OEC. Instead, one can regard our method as a better initialization point than pure BC in OEC.

Appendix G Anatomy of an LLM agent’s rollout

This appendix illustrates how a ReAct-style rollout decomposes into actions, observations, and tokens, instantiating the formalism in §2.1. Figure 7 shows a single rollout on one of our HotpotQA training questions: a system prompt and question followed by alternating agent turns (thinking and tool-call segments) and environment observations (tool responses), with token IDs annotated so the next-token-prediction target is explicit. Figure 8 re-draws the same trajectory as a linearized sequential decision process: the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} emits each action ata_{t} autoregressively conditioned on the growing history ht−1=(q,a1,o1,…,at−1,ot−1)h_{t-1}=(q,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}), and the dashed box marks the next-step prediction target supervised at training time.

Appendix H Example On-Policy Agent Trajectory

We attach one example of on-policy agent trajectory which is used in Terminal-Bench-Dev task for OP-Short. The prefix model is SFT(π0,10%​𝒟BC)(\pi_{0},10\%\mathcal{D}_{\text{BC}}), student model is Qwen3-8B and teacher model is GLM 4.6. Note we sometimes also call prefix model "student model" in certain context, people should be clear about the usage. We choose this trajectory because this task cannot be marked complete either in 𝒟BC\mathcal{D}_{\text{BC}} or when prefix model is Qwen3-8B as well.

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
namespace Tests.Infrastructure
{
class NetworkHandler : HttpMessageHandler, IDisposable
{
public Uri Address { get; set; }
public HttpContent Content { get; set; }
public IDictionary<string, object> Properties { get; set; }
private HttpResponseMessage _responseMessage;
private bool _disposed = false;
protected override Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
Address = request.RequestUri;
Content = request.Content;
Properties = request.Properties;
// Dispose previous response if exists
_responseMessage?.Dispose();
_responseMessage = new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.NotFound);
return Task.FromResult(_responseMessage);
}
public void Dispose()
{
Dispose(true);
GC.SuppressFinalize(this);
}
protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)
{
if (!_disposed)
{
if (disposing)
{
_responseMessage?.Dispose();
}
_disposed = true;
}
}
}
}
